intro: Walter Morse Rummel, a pianist closely associated with Debussy, recorded Chopin’s Waltz in C♯ minor, Op. 64 No. 2, in January 1943. The piece moves between a chordal melody, a running refrain and a slower song in D♭ major.

sections.label: A · Chordal opening melody, C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Long notes alternate with short right-hand flourishes.

sections.label: B · Quavers over the waltz bass
sections.mNote: The right hand plays quick descending phrases.

sections.label: C · Longer phrases and descending tune
sections.mNote: Longer phrases alternate with the descending tune.

sections.label: D · Opening melody, C♯ minor
sections.mNote: Paired notes and short flourishes return in C♯ minor.

sections.label: E · Final running tune, più mosso
sections.mNote: Più mosso leads to the last C♯ minor chords

cues.title: Opening melody in two voices
cues.text: Chopin writes the opening melody in paired notes, with one voice sustained beneath the other. Small flourishes decorate the line while the bass keeps its waltz pattern. At the first change of pace, Più mosso, the upper voice runs down in quavers.
cues.evidence: Score, opening Tempo giusto and first Più mosso; Knute Snortum engraving (2023), p. 1. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meeting with Paderewski, 1908
cues.text: On his way to Paris in 1908, Rummel met Paderewski in Switzerland. Paderewski liked his compositions and invited him to stay for a year as a pupil. Rummel declined and went on to Paris, where he met Debussy.
cues.evidence: Rummel’s move to Paris, encounter with Paderewski and subsequent association with Debussy: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Morse_Rummel

cues.title: Rummel’s Bach transcriptions
cues.text: Rummel also arranged for piano music written for other instruments and for voices. He transcribed organ works by Bach and Vivaldi and filled four books with piano versions of movements from Bach’s cantatas, in which several vocal parts are given to one pianist.

cues.title: Final Più mosso and cadence
cues.text: The quicker tune closes the waltz in C♯ minor. Its slurred quavers descend across the three beats of the bass, and upward runs start each phrase again. The waltz ends on a right-hand leap and a left-hand chord.
cues.evidence: Score, final Più mosso and cadence, p. 5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/28/IMSLP879636-PMLP2373-waltz-op64-no2.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
